IME, the biggest source of rework cost that happens at (or after) code review is when someone notices that the code, correctly or not, implements the wrong thing. For example, the feature, as implemented, doesn’t sufficiently solve the original business problem. Or it solves it in a bad way, like because of overengineering or taking on unnecessary technical debt. I haven’t really seen much evidence of AI code review catching either of these problems.

I’ve heard people complain that human code review doesn’t reliably catch them, either. And I have seen that with my own eyes. Just not universally. Teams that have a strong culture of shared ownership and collaborating on designs regularly catch these kinds of problems in code review. If they’re really good at it, they catch them even earlier. e.g., I know planning poker isn’t fashionable anymore, but when I’ve been on teams that take it seriously they tend to be pretty good at finding minimally expensive, correct designs pretty early in the process. Which makes both coding snd code review go faster because simpler designs are easier to manage. And design flaws that do make it to code review tend to be smaller and less expensive to fix. So those teams didn't tend to bottleneck on code review in the first place.

But I think the reason that Berger focuses on the critical class analysis of art is in the title. He's mainly focused on unpacking the way "fine art" gets valued and how/who those ideas of what is desirable, beautiful, etc were shaped. Then he ties that to the way the modern ruling class of his time used art to shape what is valued and desired with the tech/economic advancements at the time.

So focusing on the beauty of specific pieces wasn't really the focus of his work, as I imagine plenty of other contemporaries were already covering that.

As an artist I also don't think that it necessarily takes away from the art to acknowledge that what I make is shaped by my need to also make money and the markets they exist in affect that. I think it can be equally true that the impressionists were capturing nostalgic scenes of everyday life in a novel way that that people would want to buy, but that also was a product of people similarly working within what would sell in a market (which would be an advancement on previous conditions where people could even choose to pursue that kind of life which is revolutionary for the time).

He even acknowledges how his book is only the start of an analysis and it would be neat to see someone pick up this work not just from the perspective of the ruling class that commissioned the art but also the artists who made it and their stories. Obviously a lot of that gets lost with history though so that's probably harder to do.

nginx -> puma/unicorn/gunicorn/etc -> your code

With cgi that middle layer is gone. It's just:
